title: Case 2: who gets power after a fault?
points: A fault removes a supply path. Available capacity limits what can be restored.
The operator sets priorities; the agent can request and check restoration options.
note:
Plain-language explanation: A fault removes one normal supply path. Alternative paths have limited capacity, so the operator must choose what to restore. Serving critical demand first can differ from maximizing the total power served. The agent can carry that priority into a study request, collect the result and request a new study when the situation changes.

Original source detail: This six-node graph is separate from the voltage feeder. It represents active-power transport, not AC power flow or a time-ordered field switching procedure. Loads are picked up as whole blocks. A tie is an alternative connection that can supply load; CAPACITIES_KW sets its transfer limit in kilowatts.
caption: Six-node lab graph. Cyan marks critical loads; dashed links are backup options.

title: How the agent helps restore service
points: Choose the goal: critical loads first, or the most total power.
The agent can request a study, read the trade-off and ask for a new study when limits change.
note:
Plain-language explanation: The operator supplies the goal. The numerical solver chooses loads under the network rules. An agent could manage the study request and read its result, but it should not invent the service priority. L6 runs the tools directly; the recorded agent example comes later.

Original source detail: Critical demand totals 90 kW: 60 kW at node 2 and 30 kW at node 5. The objective is the service goal encoded as a score. The priority score gives more weight to these critical loads, while the comparison score maximizes total kW. The difference in selected service comes from that goal. Both numerical methods use the same graph, capacities and whole-load pickup rules. Neither needs a language model to solve this declared problem.
caption: Concept map. L6 runs the solver directly; L10B replays a separate saved agent study.

title: L6: compare two restoration goals
points: Run L6 to choose which loads receive power under each goal.
MILP chooses whole loads; a separate calculation checks its result.
note: MILP means mixed-integer linear programming. Here it is a whole-load chooser: on/off choices decide which load blocks are served, while linear constraints enforce the stated network rules. Start with tie capacities of 40, 60, 80, 100 and 120 kW. The solver enforces active-power balance, capacity limits, connection to a source, no loops in the energized graph, and exclusion of the faulted branch. An independent exhaustive search checks the priority score on this small graph. Agreement supports this formulation; it does not check the AC physics left out of the model.
code_display_caption: Colab L6 / run the whole cell

title: Read total and critical service
points: Left: all power restored. Right: power restored to critical loads.
Overlapping markers mean the two goals give the same result.
note: The markers show sampled capacities rather than a continuous ramp between whole-load pickup plans. A higher capacity may still be too small to add another complete load block. Read both total and critical service before choosing the policy that matches the request.
caption: Reference L6 results. Both goals use the same network.

title: The service goal changes who gets power
points: Critical-first goal: 130 kW total, including 90 kW critical.
Most-total-power goal: 140 kW total, including 30 kW critical.
note: Compare the first two output rows, where tie_capacity_kw=40. The priority plan serves 10 kW less total demand while preserving 60 kW more critical demand. These results compare two service objectives, not AI with no AI.
caption: Reference L6 output at the 40 kW tie setting.

title: Check the restoration plan
points: Keep the faulted branch out of service.
Check supply paths, capacity and totals before accepting the plan.
note:
Plain-language explanation: The result must respect the unavailable faulted branch and the model’s supply and capacity rules. A field switching sequence needs additional operating work.

Original source detail: Numerical checks and same-content evidence matching answer different questions. A record can match the inputs exactly while still omitting AC voltage, reactive-power or protection limits. Comparing the MILP score with every permitted plan is an independent check of this small stated problem. Minimizing energized branches does not calculate the number or order of physical switching steps.
caption: Checks on the active-power model. AC and field-operation checks remain separate.

title: Exercise 2: increase tie capacity
points: Add 180. to CAPACITIES_KW. Keep 40. first. Predict, then rerun L6.
Compare total and critical power at 40 and 180 kW.
At which tested capacity do the two goals first give the same result?
note: Three minutes to predict, edit and run; debrief on the following one-minute answer slide. Allow one minute to predict, two minutes to edit and run, and one minute to report. At 180 kW, both methods serve 250 kW total and 90 kW critical demand. Keep 40 kW first in the list because L7 binds the first result to the first capacity. Do not reorder the list for this exercise.

title: Exercise 2 answer: capacity changes the trade-off
points: At 40 kW, the priority goal serves 90 kW critical instead of 30 kW, with less total service.
The goals first match at the tested 80 kW. At 180 kW, both serve 250 kW total and 90 kW critical.
note: At 40 kW tie capacity, priority-weighted MILP serves 130 kW total and 90 kW critical. The unweighted maximum-kW policy serves 140 kW total and 30 kW critical. In the sampled list, outcomes first match at 80 kW; they also match at 100, 120 and 180 kW. At 180 kW, both serve 250 total and 90 critical kW. Do not infer the exact continuous crossover from this discrete sweep. Keep 40 first, restore the original list and rerun L6 before L7.

title: More capacity can remove this trade-off
points: At 180 kW, both goals give the same result.
The chosen priority matters when capacity forces a choice.
note: Compare the 180 kW result with the 40 kW case before generalizing. Equal service at 180 kW follows from this small graph and its demands; it is not a universal threshold. A single success percentage would hide the service-policy question.

title: L7: change the request, then check the evidence
points: Restore the original capacity list and rerun L6.
Run L7: the requested capacity changes from 40 kW to 20 kW.

title: The old result no longer matches
points: The original request matches; the changed request does not.
Put the old recommendation on HOLD and request a new calculation.

note: This output reports evidence binding, not physical infeasibility. A separate fresh solve at 20 kW still gives the 130 kW total and 90 kW critical priority outcome on this graph. L7 itself does not run that solve. Replace the stale evidence because it belongs to a different request, even when the old plan might remain feasible.

title: A new limit needs a new study
points: Old evidence does not tell us whether a new plan works.
Calculate again, check again and attach the new result to the new request.
source_label: Classroom_Labs.ipynb, L7; cell classroom-021; request/evidence binding.
note:
Plain-language explanation: An agent can notice the changed request, ask the tool to solve it again and return the new checks. Rewriting the old explanation would not update the calculation.

Original source detail: Evidence binding asks whether a record matches the exact request, proposed plan and returned result. The diagram’s extra topology labels are teaching illustrations. The runnable L7 example changes only the request capacity and revision; students do not change topology in that cell. Old evidence is unusable for a changed request even if the old plan might still pass its limits. Ask which new numerical check would establish that for the changed request.
caption: A failed input match asks for a new study; it does not establish physical infeasibility.

title: The agent keeps the operator’s goal
points: The operator sets priorities. The solver selects loads.
The agent can request the solve and explain the returned service trade-off.
note: This is a proposed role for an agent, not a new model decision in the default notebook. The current supervisor is ordinary Python. A future language-model agent could request the allowed solve and explain the returned tradeoff. It must preserve the operator’s service goal and limits, rather than quietly changing weights or making up load values. A different service goal requires an explicit new request and solve. The numerical difference here comes from the optimization objective.
caption: Proposed agent use. L6 itself runs Python.

title: This model leaves some checks for later
points: This small model checks which loads receive power.
Voltage, protection and field switching need separate checks.
note: State this boundary clearly and briefly. The result is useful within its declared transport formulation. Actual restoration requires the utility's engineering checks, operating procedure and separate authority.
